name: Sea Island Creole English

ancestors.notes: Descent per Glottolog classification of Sea Island Creole English (gull1241).
English superstrate/lexifier of Gullah, from the English of Sea Island coastal-Carolina/Georgia planters and traders (Turner 1949).

Kikongo (Kongo) substrate, one of the West African source languages named by APiCS (survey ch. 13, apics-online.info/surveys/13: 'Fula, Kongo, Mende, Vai, Yoruba') as figuring prominently in the texts, personal names and words Turner (1949) collected; no source ranks it as the largest single contributor.

Fula (Fulani) substrate, named in APiCS survey ch. 13 (apics-online.info/surveys/13); Wikipedia additionally records Gullah speakers who could recite songs and do simple counting in Fulani alongside Mende and Vai (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gullah_language).
Yoruba substrate, named in APiCS survey ch. 13 (apics-online.info/surveys/13) among the West African languages prominent in Turner's (1949) Gullah word/name corpus.

notes: English-lexifier creole of the South Carolina and Georgia Sea Islands, written in a Latin, largely English-based spelling. Klein (2013, APiCS ch. 13, synthesising Turner 1949, Jones-Jackson 1978 and Weldon 2004) gives a 12-monophthong system with close/open pairs at each height (i/ɪ, u/ʊ, e/ə, ɛ/ʌ/ɔ, a/ɑ) and lists ɹ (not a trill) as the rhotic approximant; the single-letter vowel graphemes here (a, e, i, o, u) are mapped to the close/back member of each pair (ɑ, e, i, o, u) rather than the lax member an English-orthography reading would suggest, because that is the value the wikipron gold consistently aligns to for plain vowel letters (measured from the cached gold, not itself sourced choice-by-choice — the orthography cannot distinguish the contrastive pair from spelling alone, so this is the closest reachable approximation, not a claim that Gullah lacks the lax vowels). th is stopped categorically per Klein/Turner: voiceless [t] elsewhere, voiced [d] in the closed set of English function words (the, this, that, these, those, they, them, their, then, than, though, thus) where English has ð, listed as word_exceptions because the orthography does not otherwise mark the θ/ð contrast. Gullah has no fixed standard orthography and much text is eye-dialect respelling of English; unstressed-vowel reduction, vowel length, nasalisation and any prosodic detail are not recoverable from plain-letter spelling and are left unencoded, so a real PER floor is expected.

sources.title: Africanisms in the Gullah Dialect
sources.notes: Foundational documentation of Gullah's West African substrate: nearly 4,000 items of African origin (loanwords, personal names, story/song fragments) traced to languages including Kongo, Fula, Mende, Vai and Yoruba.

sources.title: Gullah (Survey chapter 13, structure and phonology)
sources.publisher: In: Michaelis, S.M., Maurer, P., Haspelmath, M. & Huber, M. (eds.), Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures Online, chapter 13, Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology
sources.notes: Names Fula, Kongo, Mende, Vai and Yoruba as the West African substrate languages figuring prominently in Turner's (1949) Gullah word/name corpus (does not rank them by lexical contribution). Table 1 (Vowels), citing Turner [1949] 2002, Jones-Jackson 1978 and Weldon 2004, gives the 12 core monophthongs i/u, ɪ/ʊ, e/ə/o, ɛ/ʌ/ɔ, a/ɑ. Table 2 (Consonants) lists the rhotic as an approximant ɹ (not a trill) and states 'English [θ] and [ð] appear categorically as [t] and [d], respectively.'
